items.prompt: Two processes both have a pointer with the same value, 0x7fff1000. Why doesn't reading through it in process A ever accidentally return data from process B?
choices: The OS randomizes pointer values so they never collide
Each process has its own page table — the same virtual address maps to a different (or no) physical location per process
Processes share physical memory directly, but the CPU blocks cross-process reads in hardware
It's mostly coincidence — occasionally it does leak data between processes
items.explanation: Addresses are never physical from a process's point of view. The MMU translates every virtual address through that specific process's page table, so identical virtual addresses in two processes almost always resolve to entirely different physical memory — often none at all.

items.prompt: A program dereferences a NULL pointer and crashes immediately instead of silently reading garbage data. Why?
choices: NULL is a special CPU instruction that always crashes
Address 0x0 is deliberately left unmapped in the process's page table, so any access to it faults
The compiler inserts a runtime check before every pointer dereference
RAM physically has no data at address 0, so the CPU errors automatically
items.explanation: Leaving 0x0 unmapped is a deliberate OS/loader decision, not a hardware property of RAM — it turns a whole class of bugs (using a pointer before it's set to something real) into an immediate, loud fault instead of a silent read of unrelated memory.

items.prompt: Why does Unix process creation split into two separate steps — fork() then exec() — instead of one combined "start_process()" call?
choices: Historical accident with no real benefit today
Splitting them lets code run in the child (e.g. redirecting file descriptors) after duplication but before the new program's code takes over
fork() is faster than exec(), so splitting them improves performance
exec() requires superuser permissions and fork() doesn't
items.explanation: The gap between fork() and exec() is exactly where a shell sets up things like output redirection (> file, | pipe) — code the shell controls runs there, in the child, before the child's identity is replaced by the new program.

items.prompt: L3 showed a stack limit turning unbounded recursion into a catchable error rather than a silent runaway. Write willStackOverflow(currentDepth, frameSizeBytes, stackLimitBytes) that returns true once the recursion would exceed the stack's size.

tests.description: exactly at the limit is not yet an overflow
one frame past the limit overflows

items.explanation: This is the same arithmetic the runtime is implicitly doing when it decides to throw "Maximum call stack size exceeded": total space used so far (depth × cost per frame) compared against the reserved stack size. It's `>` and not `>=` because using exactly the full budget hasn't overflowed it yet — the next frame would.
